in_context.text: Paul has just warned against false teachers who treat godliness as a way to get rich, and against the love of money (6:3-10). He then turns to Timothy: flee these things, pursue godly virtues (6:11), and keep up the struggle of faith, holding on to the eternal life God called him to.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in Paul's name. Others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus. Paul calls him "O man of God" in the verse before.

what.text: Paul gives Timothy two commands: keep competing in the contest of faith, and take firm hold of eternal life. He reminds Timothy that God called him to this life and that he once made a public confession of faith before many witnesses. The text does not say when or where that confession took place.

events.text: The verse looks back to an earlier public confession by Timothy. The sources do not date that event.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: Timothy was leading the church in Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where Paul wrote from is not stated, though he had gone on to Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul wants Timothy to stand apart from greedy, quarrelsome teachers. He should not chase riches. He should press on in faith and stay faithful until Christ appears.

big_picture.text: The letter teaches that sound belief and godly living belong together. The same picture of a contest appears elsewhere: "I have fought a good fight" (2 Timothy 4:7).

for_readers.text: The "fight" here is the steady effort of living out faith. That means fleeing greed and pursuing righteousness, love, patience, and meekness. It is not a fight against people.

misuse.popular_reading: Often quoted as a general battle cry for any struggle, or as permission to be combative and argue hard for one's views.

in_context_reading.text: In context, Timothy is told to withdraw from "strifes of words" and disputes (6:4-5) and to pursue meekness (6:11). The struggle Paul has in mind is to keep the faith and godly character, not to quarrel.

why_it_matters.text: Agōn first meant a gathering for games, then a contest, struggle, or trial. The lexicon lists this verse where it describes the Christian life as a contest and struggle.
The word means to grasp or seize hold of. The same phrase about eternal life appears again in 6:19, where it is tied to being rich in good works.
This word is used of God inviting people into the blessings of his kingdom. The eternal life Timothy grasps is one God first called him to.
The word means a confession. The same word is used in the next verse for Christ's "good confession" before Pontius Pilate, which links Timothy's public stand to Jesus' own.

takeaway.text: This verse calls a believer to keep going, like an athlete who does not quit. That means turning from greed and quarrels, holding firmly to the life God offers, and staying true to what one has openly confessed.

resolved.reason: No cited source says 2 Timothy 4:7 was written near the end of Paul's life. Treating Paul as its author also passes over the authorship debate noted in the sources.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources

resolved.reason: The lexicon gives 'contest, struggle' with no contrast to warfare. The same letter even uses 'war a good warfare' (1:18), so 'rather than warfare against enemies' goes beyond the sources.

resolved.reason: Saying the word 'mainly' pictures an athlete's contest overstates the lexicons. They also give 'to fight, struggle, strive' and 'contest, struggle, trial' without naming athletics as the main sense here.
